mcqs.question: Memoizing naive recursive Fibonacci changes its time complexity from O(2ⁿ) to O(n). What is the mechanism behind that improvement?
options: Every distinct subproblem is computed exactly once and cached, instead of the exponential tree recomputing the same subproblems repeatedly
The recursion depth itself is reduced from n to log n
Memoization changes the recurrence from two branches to one branch per call
The cache eliminates the need for a base case
mcqs.explanation: The exponential blowup in naive Fibonacci comes entirely from recomputing the same smaller subproblems over and over across the tree — memoization doesn't change the recursive structure or reduce branching, it just ensures each of the n distinct subproblems is solved once and reused, collapsing exponential redundant work into linear unique work.

mcqs.question: Memoized Fibonacci uses O(n) cache memory plus O(n) stack space, compared to naive Fibonacci's O(n) stack space alone. Why is this still considered a good trade?
options: Because the memoized version has strictly better space complexity too
Because memoization removes the need for recursion entirely
Because it isn't a good trade — the naive version should be preferred when memory matters
Because a modest, linear O(n) increase in memory buys an exponential-to-linear drop in time, from O(2ⁿ) down to O(n)
mcqs.explanation: Memoized Fibonacci trades a modest O(n) extra cache for collapsing O(2ⁿ) time down to O(n), an enormous win for a small, linear memory cost. The naive version's only 'advantage' is skipping that O(n) cache, which is rarely worth an exponential time penalty — and its space complexity isn't actually better, since both versions use O(n) stack space.

mcqs.question: When does precomputing a full lookup table (like a prime sieve) beat computing each answer on demand?
options: When the number of queries against the same fixed input universe is large relative to the table's build cost
Only when the input size n is small
Always — precomputation is asymptotically superior to on-demand computation in every case
Only when the queries arrive in sorted order
mcqs.explanation: Precomputation pays for itself when its one-time build cost is amortized across many subsequent O(1) queries; if only a few queries will ever be made, computing on demand is cheaper overall since you never pay for answers you don't need. It isn't universally better, and query order or input size alone don't determine the trade-off.

mcqs.question: A hash table turns an O(n) linear scan into an O(1) average lookup. What is it actually spending to achieve that?
options: Nothing measurable — hash tables have no meaningful overhead versus arrays
Extra CPU time only, with identical memory usage to a plain array
It only works by first sorting the data, which is the real cost
Extra memory per entry (key plus value, plus spare capacity to keep the load factor low) and the compute cost of hashing on every operation
mcqs.explanation: A hash table reserves capacity beyond its current entry count to keep collisions manageable, stores each key alongside its value rather than relying on implicit position, and pays a hash-function cost on every insert and lookup — all real costs traded for the average O(1) access. It has nothing to do with sorting.

mcqs.question: What distinguishes a strong interview answer that reaches for a hash map from a weaker one?
options: The strong answer avoids hash maps whenever possible since they're considered a code smell
The strong answer names the concrete space cost and lookup-speed gain, not just 'I'll use a hash map for O(1) lookup'
The strong answer always builds the hash map from scratch instead of using the language's built-in type
There's no meaningful difference as long as the hash map produces a correct result
mcqs.explanation: Naming the actual trade — extra O(n) memory in exchange for O(1) average lookup instead of O(n) scanning, and why that's worth it in this specific context — signals deliberate reasoning about the trade-off rather than reaching for a hash map reflexively because it's the 'usual' fast option.

mcqs.question: A prime-checking function will be called exactly once, for a single n up to 10¹². Why would precomputing a full sieve up to n be the wrong choice here?
options: A sieve up to 10¹² would need roughly a terabyte of memory, while a single O(√n) trial-division check runs in about 10⁶ operations — the query volume doesn't justify the memory cost
Sieves only work for values of n below 10⁶
Trial division is always faster than a sieve regardless of query count
Precomputation is never appropriate for prime-checking problems
mcqs.explanation: The trade-off should be sized against actual query volume: a one-time terabyte-scale precomputation to answer a single query is a wildly bad trade, while trial division answers that one query directly in about a million operations — well under a second. With many repeated queries against the same bound, the calculus would flip toward precomputing.
